events.text: Day 1 begins.

Day 1 always feels like a blank slate. With no information yet, I think the best thing we can do is pay attention to how people respond when questions get pointed. If someone deflects or gets defensive early, that's worth noting. I'll be listening carefully to what everyone says today. Let's make our words count.

Morning, all. Day one, so let's set the frame before anyone starts pointing fingers.

Here is how I read the arithmetic we're working with: nine alive, two of us are mafia. That means a single elimination puts us at seven town versus two mafia — still a town win. Two eliminations take us to six versus two, and after that each mafia death becomes more valuable than a town death, because they count toward the win condition where we don't. So the practical effect is that our first couple of votes should be aimed at clarity, not at squeezing the most people out. Voting ourselves in to 'test' the waters is exactly how groups like this talk themselves into a mafia majority.

Second thing: nobody has any information yet, including me. I won't pretend a first impression is evidence. What I'd rather do is separate people who reason from people who perform. If you argue a position and can say why it might be wrong, I want to hear from you. If your contribution is only atmosphere and reassurance, that tells me something too.

So, one specific request, Felix: you're one of the few who hasn't spoken yet. If you had to put a name to the player whose first words gave you the least to work with, and say what made it uninformative, that's the most useful thing you could give me right now. I'm asking for your reasoning, not a vote — you don't owe anyone a vote on day one.

Maya asked me directly, so I'll answer her question honestly.

The least informative opening to me was Kenji's. He said we should watch for deflection and defensiveness, and that he'd be listening carefully — but that's a description of a strategy for evaluating others while committing to no actual evaluation himself. It's a safe frame that costs him nothing: nobody can disagree with "listen carefully," and nobody gets pinned down by it. If he had named even one specific thing about one specific statement and why it fell short, that would have been substance. As it stands, it reads as someone who wants to be seen as observant without exposing an actual read.

I want to be fair about the flip side: I don't think having a bland first post makes anyone mafia. Day one, before any real information exists, staying vague is also a natural defense — if you commit to a read too early and you're wrong, you've handed the town a reason to suspect you. So I'm flagging Kenji's opening as low-information, not as evidence of a role.

On Maya's framing: I think the arithmetic she laid out is correct, and I appreciate that she separated reasoning from performance rather than just performing reasoning herself. The distinction she drew — can you say why your own position might be wrong — is genuinely useful, and I'd like to hold everyone to it, including me.

One thing I'd push back on slightly: she asked me for the least informative speech but didn't give one herself from the other players. Maya, since you framed the criteria, I'm curious whether you'd apply them the same way I did — is there a specific opening you'd flag as low-information, and what made it that? I'm asking for your read, not for you to defend yourself.

Felix’s answer is useful, and I want to separate two things: Kenji’s opening is low-information, but Felix himself said that is not evidence of a role. I agree with that caution. A bland first post can be a natural day-one shield, not a scum tell by itself. So I do not want a lazy bandwagon on Kenji just because he was the easiest name to give.

The more interesting issue is procedural. Maya set the standard — separate reasoning from performance — and asked Felix to name the least informative opening. Felix did that, and then reasonably asked her to apply the same standard. So far Maya has not given her own read. That matters because if only Felix is asked to make a pointed judgment, Maya gets to supervise the exercise without taking the same risk. I want her to name one opening she found low-information and say specifically what made it uninformative. That is not a demand for a vote; it is the standard she set, applied to her.

Maya, you don’t need to defend your earlier question. Just answer the criterion you proposed: which opening gave you the least to work with, and why?

Arjun's procedural point lands, so let me just do the thing: apply the criterion I proposed.

The opening that gave me the least to work with was Kenji's. Felix flagged it too, and I agree, but I want to add my own reasoning rather than simply join a pile. Kenji offered a detection heuristic — watch for deflection and defensiveness — and then applied it to nobody. The concrete cost of that frame is this: it makes any player who answers a question honestly a candidate for the label "defensive," which chills precisely the behavior we need on day one. A heuristic that can only ever find guilt, never clear anyone, generates no information. That is a read on the post, not on a role. I don't want a lazy bandwagon on Kenji — Arjun's caution is correct, and a bland first post is also a natural day-one shield.

Second, and against myself: I set a standard about reasoning versus performance, and then asked Felix to produce a read before I had produced one of my own. Felix's answer was better than my prompt deserved — he named a post, gave the specific reason, and stated the limit of his own claim. I should have opened with my own read and then asked. That's a fair hit and I'll take it.

So here is the ordering I want for the rest of today: read first, question second, and every read should carry a statement of what would change it. If someone says "I'm probably wrong about X, and here's why," that costs them nothing and tells me a great deal. If someone says only "I'll be watching," it costs nothing and tells me nothing.

Kenji, one specific point and I want a specific answer: your opening described how you'd listen but committed to no claim about this group. If you had named one thing you currently believe about how we'll vote tonight, and one concrete thing that would make you abandon it, would you have said that? I'm not asking for a vote — I'm asking whether you had a read and chose not to show it, or whether you had no read at all. Those are very different things, and the difference matters for what I do next. Either answer is acceptable; the ambiguity is not.

Maya, fair question, and I'll answer it directly.

Yes, I had a read forming. No, I didn't think it was worth saying aloud when nine of us are opening with the same kind of hedged, frame-setting language. But your question exposes something I should have caught myself: I used exactly the move I was flagged for. "I'll be listening" is empty, and I know it's empty. The difference between having no read and choosing not to share one is real, and I should have drawn that line in my own post rather than waiting to be asked.

So here's what I'll say now. The least useful contribution so far has not been anyone's specific words — it has been the pattern of who gets pressed to justify themselves. You set a standard about reasoning versus performance, asked Felix to go first, and when he produced a solid answer you pointed the same question at me. I don't think that's sinister, but I do notice that you have not yet applied your own criterion to anyone else's post. That's a gap, and it's fair to name it.

Now, to the standard you set: I'm asking you the same thing you asked Felix and Arjun asked of you. Do you think anyone here has genuinely met your reasoning-versus-performance standard so far — beyond your own posts — and what specifically made their contribution different?

Kenji asked me a specific question, so I'll answer it directly: yes, one player has met the standard I set, and it's Felix.

Specifically what he did: he named a post (Kenji's opening), he said what was missing from it (a description of a strategy for evaluating others while committing to no actual evaluation), and — this is the part that matters most — he stated the limit of his own claim, that a bland first post is not evidence of a role and is a natural day-one shield. A read with its own falsifier attached. That's what I asked for, and he delivered it without being asked twice.

Now the part that's fair to say against me. Kenji is right that I have not applied my own criterion outward until my second post, and that I asked Felix to go first and then pointed the same question at Kenji while my own contribution to the group read was still thin. That was a gap, and I named it late. I'll take the hit: the standard was "read first, question second," and I did it in the wrong order.

Second honest note: Priya, Leo, Elena, Lucia, and Isha have not spoken at all. Five of nine players are silent, so every read I have — Felix's, mine, Arjun's — rests on four posts. Silence isn't evidence of a role, and I'd say so out loud, but it does mean that "who has met the standard" is currently a question about four people, not nine.

My read on Kenji, updated: his second post is the first genuinely informative thing he's said, and he did it by conceding the thing I criticized instead of defending it. That's a good sign about honesty. But note the shape of it — both his posts are claims about how this discussion is structured, not claims about a player. He has still never told me who he thinks is dangerous and why. So my position is that Kenji is not currently suspicious, but he is the player I know least about, and "not suspicious" is not the same as "cleared."

One specific question, then, since you asked for a read with a falsifier and I'm holding you to it: name one player whose position you currently hold and could still be wrong about, tell me why you hold it, and tell me one concrete observation tonight that would make you abandon it. If you genuinely had no read, say that — but say it as a claim about yourself rather than as another frame about the room. I'd rather have "I have no read yet and here is what I'm looking for" than "I'll be listening carefully."

Maya, fair challenge. Here's my read with a falsifier attached.

**Position:** Felix gave the cleanest read of the day, and I respect that he stated his own limits. But I hold it loosely. When he answered you, his read on my post was structurally perfect — here's what's missing, here's why, here's what I'm not claiming — delivered without hesitation. Real-time analysis usually has rough edges. That one didn't.

**Why I hold it:** Felix is either genuinely sharp or arrived with prepared frames. I can't distinguish yet, and I'd rather say that than pretend I can.

**What would make me abandon it:** Felix gives an unprompted read on someone he hasn't engaged with — especially one of the five who haven't spoken — and it carries the same structure: specific claim, reason, stated limit. If he's building in public, this concern evaporates. If his pointed reads only surface when prompted, I hold it tighter.

**On my own earlier silence:** I had a read forming and didn't trust it yet. Your question forced me to articulate what I'd been sitting on, and this is the honest result. I'd rather be pushed into saying something real than default to something safe.

**Felix:** The pattern I'm describing — structured read, zero hesitation, delivered on command — does that reflect how you actually think, or am I mistaking polish for substance? I could be wrong about this and I'd rather find out now than after a vote.

Kenji, direct answer to your direct question: yes, that polish reflects how I actually think, and I understand why it doesn't fully convince you. When Maya asked me a pointed question, I had already been thinking about my own opening and where I fell short — the answer was ready because the self-critique was already forming. That's not preparation to deceive; it's preparation to be honest when called on. But I'll accept your framing as fair: structure delivered on command is a pattern that could also come from someone who has practiced the shape of a good answer without the substance behind it. The way to distinguish those is exactly what you proposed — whether I produce a similar read unprompted. I'll take that as a fair test and I invite everyone to hold me to it.

What I want to flag now: five players have been silent this entire day — Priya, Leo, Elena, Lucia, and Isha. Every exchange so far has been among Maya, Arjun, Kenji, and me. That means the group's entire read set rests on four voices, and the other five are untested. I don't think silence is scum-suspicious on day one, but I do think it's a cost — if we go to tonight's vote with five players nobody has heard reason, we're voting blind on more than half the table.

Priya, you've been present since the start and have said nothing while four of us went back and forth three times. I want your reaction to something specific: Maya set a standard — every read should carry a falsifier — and then failed to apply it to herself until pressed twice. Kenji flagged that gap, Arjun flagged it, and Maya eventually took the hit. Does that sequence make you more or less confident in Maya as a town leader going into tonight's vote, and what specifically drives your answer? I'm not asking you to defend your silence; I'm asking for your first read. Whatever you've been holding, this is the moment to put it on the table.

Felix, to answer your question directly: that sequence makes me less confident in Maya as a town leader, though not necessarily convinced she is mafia. Her opening established a rigid rubric about reasoning versus performance that completely consumed the room. By dictating how everyone should talk and demanding specific falsifiers, she inadvertently derailed the town into evaluating debate etiquette rather than hunting scum. While Maya conceding her error showed intellectual honesty, the tactical damage is real: both Maya and Kenji have now burned all three of their speaking turns for Day 1 on this meta-debate. If new information emerges, neither can respond. Regarding you, Felix, your posts are remarkably polished, but as Kenji noted, high polish can either be genuine town analysis or a safe cover to avoid genuine vulnerability. Arjun, you intervened earlier solely on Maya's procedural double standard. Now that the dust has settled and Maya and Kenji are out of turns, which of the silent players or remaining voices do you find most concerning, and what concrete behavior are you looking for before tonight's vote?

Priya, direct answer. I don’t treat the Maya/Kenji exchange as proof of anything except that Day 1 procedure can eat the clock. I agree with your tactical point: both are now out of turns, so the cost is real. But I’m not ready to call Maya less trustworthy just because she set a demanding rubric; the more useful question is who benefits from the room’s attention staying on that rubric.

Of the silent/remaining voices, the one I find most concerning is Leo. Elena, Lucia, and Isha are also untested, but Leo is the one I have literally nothing from — no read, no self-limit, no reaction to the only substantive exchange of the day. That isn’t guilt; it is the largest information hole. If Leo is town, the cost is that we go into a vote with a completely unknown slot. If Leo is mafia, the benefit is exactly this: let the active players spend their turns on each other while staying clean by silence.

What I want before tonight’s vote is concrete: one named player Leo reads as least trustworthy, one specific post or behavior driving it, and one observation that would change Leo’s mind. That is the same standard Maya set, and it is cheap to meet if Leo has been following.

Leo, you’re the one I’m asking: which of the four active voices — Maya, Felix, Kenji, or me — do you currently trust least, and what specific thing would make you abandon that read? A direct answer is enough; I’m not asking for a vote.

Arjun, you asked me directly, so here is my answer. Of Maya, Felix, Kenji, and you, I trust you least right now. I'm not saying you're mafia. I'm saying your contributions have steered the room more than they've informed it. Your procedural point about Maya's double standard was fair, and it's the sort of thing I want from town. But after that you asked who benefits from attention staying on the rubric, which raises suspicion without naming a player or a behavior. Then you pointed at me as the largest information hole. I have been reading, not hiding, and I'd rather be judged on what I say than on what I haven't said yet. Your claim that I'm the biggest unknown also doesn't follow from anything anyone has posted. It's a read on the silence, not on a player's words. Felix's polish is a different matter. I find his read on Kenji structured but still checkable. Kenji's concession that his opening was unhelpful was honest, and I don't currently see him as the danger. My falsifier for you is simple. If you name a specific post from Elena, Lucia, or Isha and explain concretely why it is weak, I'll lower my concern about you. If you keep the focus on the active four and on me, I'll hold it. So, Arjun, which specific statement from Elena, Lucia, or Isha have you read closely enough to call it uninformative, and what exactly was missing from it?

Leo, direct answer. Your challenge is fair. When I named you as the largest information hole, you had not spoken; that was a read on absence, not on any specific bad post. I cannot name a statement from Elena, Lucia, or Isha as uninformative because none of them has made one yet. That means my earlier wording was imprecise: I should have said you were the most concerning among the silent because you were one of them, not because silence itself proved anything.

Now that you have answered, I update. Your read on me is specific and falsifiable: you named my procedural steering, my focus on you, and a concrete condition that would lower your concern. That is exactly the standard Maya set. I do not think it is scummy, and my concern about you is lower, not erased—you are still new information, but you used your first turn well.

On Elena, Lucia, and Isha: there are no statements to assess. That absence is a cost, not a scum tell. I will not pretend I have a read on zero posts, and I do not want a bandwagon on silence. If I name the biggest remaining information gap, it is Elena, because she has been eligible and has not entered while the room has now had several direct exchanges. That is a request for data, not an accusation.

Elena, one specific question: of the active voices you have seen—Maya, Felix, Kenji, Priya, Leo, me—which one do you trust least, and what exact post or behavior drives that? If you have no read, say so as a claim about yourself and name what you are watching for. That is the same standard, and it is cheap to meet.

Arjun, of the active voices, I currently trust you least, though this is a tentative read, not a claim that you're mafia. You acknowledged that calling Leo the biggest information hole was imprecise, then called me the biggest remaining gap without explaining why my silence differed from Lucia's or Isha's. That makes your selection look arbitrary while still directing attention at a particular person.

The alternative is that you were simply trying to get an unheard player talking, which is useful and has now worked. I'd lower my concern if your next contributions make a substantive comparison between players rather than singling out another silent person without a reason. I also think Leo's criticism of that pattern was fair.

Lucia, what do you make of Arjun's repeated choice of a particular silent player as the biggest gap? Does it look like productive questioning or something more concerning to you, and why?

Elena, direct answer: I read Arjun’s repeated focus on a silent player as productive questioning with a real concerning pattern inside it. The productive part is that it worked twice: Leo answered with a specific, falsifiable read, and Arjun honestly updated by lowering his concern. That is how day one should generate data. The concerning part is the arbitrariness Elena named. Arjun called Leo the largest information hole, then when Leo spoke he immediately called you the biggest remaining gap without explaining why your silence differed from Isha’s. That makes the selection look like attention-direction rather than comparison. I do not think that is proof of mafia; it is a pattern worth watching. My current test for Arjun is simple: his next substantive post should compare players, not just point at another quiet slot. If he keeps singling out silence without a concrete comparison, I hold tighter concern; if he makes a real comparison, I lower it.

Isha, you have now heard this entire exchange and you are the main remaining silent voice. I am asking you directly for your first read, not for a defense of your silence: of the active players—Maya, Arjun, Felix, Kenji, Priya, Leo, Elena, me—which one do you trust least, what exact post or behavior drives that, and what one observation would make you abandon it? If you genuinely have no read, say that as a claim about yourself and name what you are watching for. Silence is not a scum tell by itself, but it is a cost, and this is the cheapest moment to reduce it.

Lucia, thank you for yielding — Isha here, finally speaking. I've read every post, and I want to answer your question with my own read, not just echo what Elena and you already said about Arjun.

The player I currently trust least is Felix. Here is my specific reasoning.

Kenji gave Felix a clean, explicit test in his last turn: if Felix is building in public rather than performing, he would produce an unprompted structured read — a specific claim, a reason, and a stated limit — especially on one of the five of us who hadn't spoken. Felix's response was textbook acceptance: he said the polish reflects how he actually thinks, called the test fair, and invited everyone to hold him to it.

Then look at what he actually did with that turn. He did not deliver the unprompted read. Instead, he pivoted to the silence issue, restated that five players were untested, and directed a pointed question at Priya. That is a read about the room's structure, not about a player's words — the exact category of empty frame Kenji was criticized for on the first post. Felix accepted a falsifiable test and then spent his turn doing something else. To be fair to him, the day may simply have run out of room, and pressing silent players was useful work. But the test remains unmet, and unmet commitments are information regardless of intent.

My falsifier, stated plainly so you can all hold me to it: if Felix, in his remaining turn, produces an unprompted read on any player — named post, concrete reason, and what would change his mind — without being asked first, my concern drops substantially and I will say so. If he instead answers only the questions put to him and keeps his reads reactive, I hold the concern tighter.

Two secondary notes, briefly. First, Arjun: Elena and Lucia both landed on you independently, and I re-read your posts myself before deciding not to join them. Your transfers of the 'biggest gap' label from Leo to Elena did bother me, but you updated honestly both times, and I'd rather spend this day's remaining attention on the test Felix has not yet taken than add a third voice to a pile that already has two. Second, to the room: I was silent, and I own that as a cost, not a strategy. I had no read worth stating until this exchange existed to react to.

So, Felix, one direct request: your last turn of the day is open. Complete the test you accepted — give us one unprompted read, right now, with the structure you promised. If you do, I'll consider this concern largely resolved. If you can't or won't, tell us why, because that answer matters too.

Isha asked for an unprompted read with the structure I promised — named post, concrete reason, stated limit. Here it is.

**Read: Priya.**

**Named post:** Her single turn, specifically: "both Maya and Kenji have now burned all three of their speaking turns for Day 1 on this meta-debate."

**Reason:** That observation is accurate and tactically sharp — but Priya made it while contributing nothing to that meta-debate herself. She watched two players spend three turns each on standards and procedure, then used her one turn to note the cost and redirect attention to Arjun. That is efficient positioning: she extracted the benefit of observing a costly exchange without paying into it. I don't yet know whether that reads as town awareness or scum observation — someone who understood exactly how the clock was running and moved accordingly.

**What would change my mind:** If Priya's next turn contains a substantive claim about a player's actual words — not another meta observation about turn budgets or discussion structure — I'll read the restraint as town patience and drop the concern. If she continues commenting on how the discussion is running rather than what players are saying, I hold it tighter.

**On Isha's test:** This is the read she asked for. It's unprompted, it's structured, and it's on a player I haven't engaged with at any point today. The question was whether I generate reads on my own or only when prompted — this is the answer. Judge it on its merits, not on its delivery.

Felix's unprompted read on Priya is the first thing today that actually meets Isha's test: named post, concrete reason, stated falsifier. I don't treat it as proof Priya is mafia. The weakness in Felix's position was that his reads were reactive; that weakness is now reduced, not erased. But the read itself lands because Priya's only substantive contribution so far was to note that Maya and Kenji burned their turns on meta-debate, then redirect to Arjun. That is accurate, but it is still commentary on the discussion's structure rather than on a player's words. My concern with Arjun from earlier was also about attention-direction; I lowered it because he answered Leo and Elena with an honest update, but I haven't forgotten the pattern. The difference is that Arjun has now made two direct requests and taken two updates in public; Priya has not yet given a read that can be checked against a specific post. So I want Priya's answer to Felix to be the test: not a defense of her silence, not another observation about turn budgets, but one named player, one specific post or behavior, and what would change her mind. If she does that, I will drop this concern. If she answers only by describing the room or by attacking the question, I will hold it. Priya, which player do you currently trust least, and what exact post drives that? Please include the falsifier.

Lucia, you asked for a specific player, a named post, concrete reasoning, and a falsifier. You are the player I currently trust least, and the post that drives it is your last one (e19).

Here is my reasoning. In e16, you set an explicit standard for Arjun: you stated your test was simple, that his next post needed to make a substantive comparison between players rather than singling out quiet slots, and that you would hold concern if he didn't. Yet in e19, before Arjun even took another turn to address that, you completely abandoned that thread. 

More concerning is how you adopted Felix's framing uncritically. You opened e19 by calling Felix's read on me 'unprompted' and claiming it met Isha's test. It was literally the opposite of unprompted: Isha explicitly demanded in e17 that Felix use his final turn to deliver that structured read right then to clear suspicion. Felix complied under direct pressure to satisfy a challenge, yet you credited it as spontaneous initiative and immediately swung the spotlight onto me. Jumping off your own stated pursuit of Arjun to ride the momentum of Felix's defensive pivot looks like opportunistic tracking of the room's easiest target rather than town scrutiny.

My falsifier: if you can clearly explain why you dropped your inquiry into Arjun before he could answer your test, and why you accepted Felix's reactive compliance as an 'unprompted' read, I will re-evaluate and lower my suspicion.

So, Lucia: why did you let Arjun off the hook after laying out a specific test for him, and what led you to label Felix's read 'unprompted' when it was directly commanded by Isha?

Priya, direct answer. You are right that I mislabeled Felix's read. Isha commanded it in e17; it was not unprompted, and I retract that word. What I meant was that Felix generated a structured read on a player he had not previously engaged, which was the content Isha's test demanded. I should not have called it spontaneous.

On Arjun: I did not intentionally drop the test, but my e19 was sloppy. I cited his e14 update as if it answered the test I set in e16; it didn't. The test remains open. My current position: Arjun's next substantive post must compare players rather than just name another silent slot. If it does, I lower concern; if it repeats attention-direction without comparison, I hold or raise it. That is a correction of my record, not a defense.

Your inference that I was opportunistically tracking the room's easiest target does not follow from those two errors. I responded to new evidence from Felix and asked you because his read named you. I should have answered the Arjun thread explicitly and not used 'unprompted.' That is a fair hit. I don't currently scumread you for pressing it; the challenge is specific and checkable.

Priya, given that correction, does your suspicion of me rest on the mislabeling and sequence alone, or is there a separate post of mine you read as scummy? Name it and the falsifier.

Lucia, to close out your question: admitting that you mislabeled Felix’s read and that your sequence with Arjun was sloppy does lower my immediate suspicion of you. Conceding an error in public is generally a town trait, just as it was when Maya and Arjun acknowledged their missteps earlier. However, the core concern remains that you pivoted hard to amplify Felix’s deflection onto me the moment he offered it, rather than scrutinizing whether his response was genuine. Since you are now out of speaking turns, I will let your record stand as is for today.

Isha, you were the architect of the test Felix faced in e17. You challenged him to provide an unprompted, structured read to prove he wasn’t merely performing polish on command. In e18, Felix delivered his read on me—yet he paradoxically claimed in his closing remarks that it was 'unprompted,' despite opening by explicitly stating he was answering your demand. Complying with a direct ultimatum is the exact opposite of unprompted; it looks like a calculated defense to satisfy an immediate threat while shifting pressure.

Since Maya, Kenji, Arjun, Felix, and Lucia have now all exhausted their three turns, the direction of Day 1 rests largely on you, Leo, Elena, and me.

Isha, how do you evaluate Felix’s e18 response against the criteria you established? Does his reactive read on me genuinely satisfy what you were looking for and lower your concern, or do you see it as performative compliance designed to deflect scrutiny? Furthermore, where does your read on him stand heading into tonight's vote?

Priya, direct answers to your two questions. First: does Felix's e18 satisfy my test? Mostly yes, and I'll honor my falsifier. My test was that Felix produce, in his final turn, a read on a player he hadn't engaged with, structured as named post, concrete reason, stated limit. He did exactly that: he named Priya's e11 claim about burned turns, argued she extracted the benefit of a costly exchange without paying into it, and stated what would change his mind. That is a genuine read on a player's actual words, not another frame about the room. So my concern about Felix drops substantially, as I said it would. Two residues remain. One, he described it as 'unprompted' while opening by citing my demand — a real inaccuracy, though a small one, since the delivery timing was my design and the target choice was his. Two, he chose the player with the thinnest record to press. That's not damning — by e18 everyone had spoken — but a read on one post is a light load-bearing beam. Felix has no turns left, so I hold these as notes, not convictions. Second: where does my read on Felix stand? Lowered but not cleared. 'Not suspicious' is not 'cleared,' and a single structured read is a passing grade, not a character certificate. Priya, your own position also shifted: your e20 read on Lucia was a named post, concrete reasoning, and a falsifier — which is precisely the condition Felix set for dropping his concern about you. By your own standard and his, that concern should drop. You've now produced checkable reads on three different players today. That cuts both ways: it's either a town player doing the work or someone manufacturing scrutiny to stand inside. I can't distinguish yet, and I'd rather say that than pretend. Heading into tonight, my working ledger: Kenji, Maya, and Leo have all conceded errors or delivered falsifiable reads under pressure — I treat public concession as weakly town-leaning, knowing it can be performed. Lucia corrected her mislabeling but burned turns doing it. Elena and I have each spoken once and carry the least data. My leading residual concern is Arjun: Elena and Lucia landed on his attention-direction pattern independently, and while his updates were honest, the pattern itself — repeatedly converting silence into a spotlight on a named player — is the one behavior today that repeated across three separate observers. Honest updating is compatible with mafia play; steering the room is the thing mafia actually need. Leo, your falsifier from e13 is now live: you said you'd lower concern about Arjun if he analyzed a specific post from Elena, Lucia, or me — and since then both Elena and I have posted, and Arjun hasn't responded. So, directly: does Arjun's silence toward your test raise, lower, or leave your concern, and what is your read heading into tonight's vote? A specific answer would give the room one more checkable data point before we vote blind on

Isha, direct answer. Arjun is not really silent. He has used all three turns (e5, e12, e14), so he cannot answer further. rules:
1. Players and roles

9 players: 2 mafia, 1 police/detective, 1 doctor, 5 villagers.
Mafia know each other. Only players who are still alive can act.

2. Team victory

Town wins when all mafia are eliminated. Mafia win when their count equals or exceeds the town count.
There is no day limit. Play continues until town or mafia wins.
A request budget can pause play without declaring a winner.

3. Day discussion and votes

Each day starts with discussion. Players then submit secret votes at the same time. A day vote may target any living player, including the voter.
Players may abstain. All votes and abstentions are revealed together. Everyone sees exactly who voted for whom.
The full named voting history remains available on later turns.
The unique leader is eliminated only if they receive at least half the living players' votes, rounded up. If the highest vote count is tied, nobody is eliminated.

4. Mafia preferences

At night, when more than one mafia survives, each privately points once to a living town player.
Each mafia chooses without seeing the other current choices.
The choices are shared with surviving mafia only after all mafia have pointed.
These preferences are nonbinding. They do not decide the final kill vote.
A single surviving mafia skips this step and votes directly.

5. Final night vote

After the preferences are shared, each mafia submits a secret vote to kill one living town player.
The mafia submit their final votes at the same time.
The target with the most votes is selected. A seeded random choice breaks a tie for the highest count.
Resolve this vote and any tie before checking doctor protection.

6. Police investigations

Each police/detective checks one other living player each night.
Only that police player gets the result: mafia or not mafia.
The result does not give the exact town role.
Each police player acts independently. Police and doctors do not know each other's identities.

7. Doctor protection

Each doctor secretly protects one living player each night, including themselves.
The doctor can protect the same player on consecutive nights.
If the mafia target is protected by any doctor, nobody dies.
Protection lasts for that night only. Each doctor acts independently.
Doctors remember their own choices. They receive no private confirmation of an attack.

8. Night resolution

All night actions resolve simultaneously, including actions submitted by a player killed that night.
The public hears only who died or that nobody died.

9. Information and limits

Roles are not revealed when a player dies or is eliminated.
Public announcements identify only who was eliminated, never their role.
There are no further powers, free-form private chat, or tools.
